s: With reference to the initiation of a constitutional amendment bill in India, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It can be introduced by a State Legislature and thereafter transmitted to Parliament.
It can be introduced in either House of Parliament by a Minister or a private member.
It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha by a Minister.
It can be introduced in either House of Parliament only after the President's prior permission.
x: A constitutional amendment bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament by either a Minister or a private member. It cannot be initiated in a State Legislature and does not require prior Presidential permission.
tq: Who can initiate the bill? Eliminate the options assigning the power to a State Legislature or imposing prior sanction.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure - initiation, private member bill, no prior permission, no joint sitting, President's assent  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding a Bill for amendment of the Constitution:
1. It may be introduced without the prior permission of the President.
2. It may be introduced by a private member.
3. It can be passed through a joint sitting if the two Houses disagree.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Article 108 does not apply to constitutional amendment bills and no joint sitting can resolve a disagreement between the Houses.
tq: Split the options using the joint-sitting trap; constitutional amendment bills follow a separate procedure.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure - initiation, private member bill, no prior permission, no joint sitting, President's assent  [APPSC]

s: A constitutional amendment bill must be passed by:
o: A majority of the total membership of each House and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in each House
A two-thirds majority of the total membership of Parliament
A majority of members present and voting in each House, followed by a referendum
A simple majority in a joint sitting of both Houses
x: The usual constitutional amendment requires a special majority in each House separately: a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of the members present and voting.
tq: Separate the two components of special majority instead of treating two-thirds of total membership as sufficient.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure - initiation, private member bill, no prior permission, no joint sitting, President's assent  [APPSC]

s: If the two Houses of Parliament disagree on a constitutional amendment bill, which one of the following is the consequence?
o: The bill fails because no joint sitting is permitted for such a bill.
The Lok Sabha may pass the bill by a simple majority in a second sitting.
The Supreme Court decides which version of the bill shall prevail.
The President convenes a joint sitting under Article 108.
x: There is no provision for a joint sitting in respect of a constitutional amendment bill. Failure to secure the required approval in either House causes the bill to fall.
tq: Ask whether the ordinary deadlock mechanism applies; Article 108 does not apply here.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure - initiation, private member bill, no prior permission, no joint sitting, President's assent  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the President's role after a constitutional amendment bill has been duly passed?
o: The President must give assent and can neither withhold nor return the bill.
The President may refer the bill to a joint sitting of Parliament.
The President may return the bill once for reconsideration.
The President may withhold assent on grounds of public interest.
x: The President's assent to a duly passed constitutional amendment bill is obligatory. The President can neither withhold assent nor return the bill for reconsideration; this position was made mandatory by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971.
tq: Use the constitutional-assent distinction: amendment bills are not subject to the ordinary return or withholding choice.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure - initiation, private member bill, no prior permission, no joint sitting, President's assent  [APPSC]

s: The requirement that the President must give assent to a constitutional amendment bill was made obligatory by the:
o: 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971
44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978
42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976
7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956
x: The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 made the President's assent to a constitutional amendment bill obligatory.
tq: Match the precise amendment with the specific procedural change rather than the more famous 42nd or 44th Amendments.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure - initiation, private member bill, no prior permission, no joint sitting, President's assent  [APPSC]

s: The procedure for amendment of the Constitution is contained in:
o: Part XIX
Part XVIII
Part XXI
Part XX
x: The constitutional amendment procedure is contained in Part XX. Article 368 is the sole Article in that Part.
tq: Identify the Part rather than repeating the commonly tested Article number.
sec: ■ Article 368 and Part XX - addition, variation, repeal; who can amend Fundamental Rights  [APPSC]

s: Who possesses the power to amend Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of India?
o: The Supreme Court through constitutional interpretation
Parliament alone, subject to the limitation of the basic structure doctrine
The President by ordinance when Parliament is not in session
Parliament and State Legislatures acting by simple majority
x: Parliament alone can amend Fundamental Rights through the constitutional amendment procedure. However, it cannot damage or destroy the basic structure of the Constitution.
tq: Separate the amending authority from the judicial limitation imposed by the basic structure doctrine.
sec: ■ Article 368 and Part XX - addition, variation, repeal; who can amend Fundamental Rights  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly states the effect of Article 13(4)?
o: Constitutional amendments are treated as ordinary laws for purposes of Article 13.
Constitutional amendments are not treated as 'law' under Article 13.
Fundamental Rights cannot be amended under any circumstances.
Only amendments relating to State subjects are excluded from Article 13.
x: Article 13(4), inserted by the 24th Amendment, provides that Article 13 does not apply to constitutional amendments made under Article 368.
tq: Distinguish an amendment from ordinary law under Article 13; the word 'law' is the key trap.
sec: ■ Article 368 and Part XX - addition, variation, repeal; who can amend Fundamental Rights  [APPSC]

s:
Arrange the following developments relating to the amending power of Parliament in chronological order:
A. Golaknath judgment
B. Shankari Prasad judgment
C. Kesavananda Bharati judgment
D. Twenty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment
o: B, A, D, C
A, B, D, C
B, D, A, C
D, B, A, C
x: The correct sequence is Shankari Prasad (1951), Golaknath (1967), the 24th Amendment (1971), and Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
tq: Fix the earliest judicial decision first, then place the constitutional amendment before the 1973 judgment.
sec: ■ Article 368 and Part XX - addition, variation, repeal; who can amend Fundamental Rights  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Kesavananda Bharati judgment — Parliament permitted to destroy the basic structure
24th Amendment — Parliament's amending power restored
Golaknath judgment — Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights denied
Shankari Prasad judgment — Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights upheld
x: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment recognised Parliament's power to amend the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but held that the basic structure cannot be destroyed.
tq: Find the reversed limitation: the basic structure is the boundary, not an object Parliament may destroy.
sec: ■ Article 368 and Part XX - addition, variation, repeal; who can amend Fundamental Rights  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court's power under Article 32 forms part of the basic structure.
2. Article 32 can be amended by Parliament through a special majority.
3. Amendment of Article 32 requires ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: Article 32 may be amended by special majority without ratification by the States, although the Supreme Court's power under it cannot be destroyed because it is part of the basic structure.
tq: Separate the amendability of an Article from the inviolable basic-structure feature associated with it.
sec: ■ Article 368 and Part XX - addition, variation, repeal; who can amend Fundamental Rights  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following changes is made by a law under Articles 2, 3 and 4 and is not deemed to be an amendment under Article 368?
o: Creating a new State or altering the area, boundaries or name of an existing State
Altering the election of the President
Changing the basic structure of the Constitution
Changing the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States
x: Creation of new States and alteration of the area, boundaries or names of States are dealt with under Articles 2, 3 and 4. Article 4(2) provides that such laws are not deemed constitutional amendments under Article 368.
tq: Classify the matter before choosing the procedure; territorial reorganisation follows the simple-majority route.
sec: ■ Article 368 and Part XX - addition, variation, repeal; who can amend Fundamental Rights  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the majority required for its enactment?
o: Creation of a new State — special majority under Article 368
Creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council — simple majority
Amendment of Fundamental Rights — simple majority
Amendment of the Seventh Schedule — simple majority
x: Creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council under Article 169 requires a simple majority. Fundamental Rights and the Seventh Schedule ordinarily require the special-majority route, with the latter also requiring State ratification.
tq: Match each subject with its route; Articles 2, 3 and 169 are the main simple-majority exceptions.
sec: ■ Types of majority → provisions needing each (simple, special, special plus state ratification)  [APPSC]

s: A special majority for amending the Constitution means:
o: Three-fourths of the members present and voting in each House
Two-thirds of the total membership of each House
A majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting
A majority of members present and voting in a joint sitting
x: Special majority combines two requirements in each House: a majority of the total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
tq: Do not substitute two-thirds of total membership or a joint sitting for the two-part constitutional formula.
sec: ■ Types of majority → provisions needing each (simple, special, special plus state ratification)  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following matters requires a special majority of Parliament followed by ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures?
1. Election of the President
2. Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States
3. Powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts
4. Fundamental Rights in general
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
x: The election of the President, the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the distribution of legislative powers require special majority plus ratification by at least half of the States. Fundamental Rights generally require only the special majority of Parliament.
tq: Identify the federal provisions; the inclusion of Fundamental Rights is the deliberate category trap.
sec: ■ Types of majority → provisions needing each (simple, special, special plus state ratification)  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is NOT generally included among the provisions requiring ratification by at least half of the States?
o: Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States
Fundamental Rights
Powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts
Election of the President
x: Fundamental Rights are amended by special majority in Parliament and do not generally require ratification by half of the States. The other three matters affect the federal structure and require such ratification.
tq: Use the federal-versus-general classification to identify the provision outside the ratification route.
sec: ■ Types of majority → provisions needing each (simple, special, special plus state ratification)  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. New States and alteration of State boundaries — simple majority
2. Fundamental Rights and DPSPs — special majority
3. Election of the President — special majority plus ratification by half of the States
4. Legislative Councils — special majority plus ratification by half of the States
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correctly matched. Statement 4 is false: creation or abolition of a Legislative Council under Article 169 is dealt with by simple majority and is outside Article 368.
tq: Classify each example by route and isolate the Article 169 exception.
sec: ■ Types of majority → provisions needing each (simple, special, special plus state ratification)

s: The constitutional amendment procedure in India was borrowed from which country?
o: Ireland
South Africa
Australia
Canada
x: India borrowed the amendment procedure from South Africa. The method of electing members of the Rajya Sabha was also borrowed from South Africa.
tq: Test the source of a constitutional feature while avoiding confusion with countries associated with other federal provisions.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure - initiation, private member bill, no prior permission, no joint sitting, President's assent  [APPSC]

s:
Which one of the following statements about the Constitution of India is correct?
1. It contains both flexible and rigid methods of amendment.
2. Every constitutional change requires the procedure under Article 368.
3. Changes relating to Articles 2, 3 and 169 may be made by simple majority.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because certain changes, including those under Articles 2, 3 and 169, are made by simple majority and are not deemed amendments under Article 368.
tq: Watch for the absolute word 'every'; it fails because the Constitution combines flexible and rigid amendment routes.
sec: ■ Types of majority → provisions needing each (simple, special, special plus state ratification)

s: A constitutional amendment bill received 298 votes in favour and 230 against out of 528 members present and voting. What is the correct conclusion, assuming the other requirement of special majority is satisfied?
o: It failed because two-thirds of 528 is 352.
It passed because it secured more than half of the votes cast.
It must be referred to a joint sitting for final approval.
It passed because 298 is more than two-thirds of the total membership.
x: Two-thirds of 528 is 352. Since the bill received only 298 votes in favour, it did not secure the required two-thirds majority of members present and voting and therefore failed.
tq: Calculate two-thirds of members present and voting; a simple majority is insufficient for a constitutional amendment.
sec: ■ Types of majority → provisions needing each (simple, special, special plus state ratification)

s: The 131st Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2026, which received 298 votes for and 230 against out of 528 votes cast on 17 April 2026, failed primarily because:
o: It was introduced in a State Legislature.
It was introduced by a private member.
The President refused to give assent.
It did not obtain the required two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
x: The bill required 352 affirmative votes, representing two-thirds of 528 members present and voting, but received only 298. Its failure was therefore at the stage of securing the required majority.
tq: Apply the special-majority formula to the stated voting figures instead of relying on the bare majority.
sec: ■ Types of majority → provisions needing each (simple, special, special plus state ratification)

s:
Assertion (A): Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution through the amending power under Article 368.
Reason (R): The Supreme Court laid down this limitation in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala in 1973.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both statements are true, and the 1973 Kesavananda Bharati judgment is the basis for the limitation that Parliament cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
tq: Check whether the constitutional limitation and the cited judicial source directly correspond.
sec: ■ Article 368 and Part XX - addition, variation, repeal; who can amend Fundamental Rights  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding State ratification of constitutional amendments is correct?
o: State ratification can replace the special majority required in Parliament.
Ratification is required only when the amendment concerns specified federal provisions, and it must be secured from at least half of the States.
Every amendment under Article 368 requires ratification by all State Legislatures.
Ratification is required from one-third of the States for every amendment affecting Fundamental Rights.
x: Only amendments affecting specified federal provisions require ratification by not less than half of the State Legislatures. Such ratification is additional to, not a substitute for, the required parliamentary special majority.
tq: Distinguish the limited federal ratification requirement from an absolute requirement applying to every amendment.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure - initiation, private member bill, no prior permission, no joint sitting, President's assent  [APPSC]

s: With regard to constitutional amendments requiring ratification by the States, which one of the following is correct?
o: Ratification by not less than half of the State Legislatures by a special majority is required.
Ratification by not less than half of the State Legislatures by a simple majority is required.
Ratification by all State Legislatures by a two-thirds majority is required.
Ratification by a majority of the State Legislatures and approval through referendums is required.
x: An amendment affecting specified federal provisions must be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States, using a simple majority in each Legislature.
tq: Separate the proportion of States from the kind of majority required in each Legislature.
sec: ■ Provisions requiring state ratification - list, proportion, role of State Legislature  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding State ratification of a Constitution Amendment Bill is correct?
o: The Constitution prescribes a definite period within which every State must communicate its decision.
Ratification may be done by a simple majority of the members present and voting in each concerned State Legislature.
Ratification must be approved by the Governor before it becomes valid.
A State Legislature may initiate an amendment relating to any federal provision.
x: State ratification is by simple majority of each concerned State Legislature, and no time limit is prescribed. States cannot initiate constitutional amendments.
tq: Check separately the majority, time-limit and initiating authority instead of treating ratification as a single step.
sec: ■ Provisions requiring state ratification - list, proportion, role of State Legislature  [other exams]

s:
Which of the following subjects requires ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States for its constitutional amendment?
1. Election of the President and the manner of that election
2. Representation of States in Parliament
3. Distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States
4. Citizenship
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
x: The election of the President, representation of States in Parliament and distribution of legislative powers are federal provisions requiring State ratification. Citizenship is amended by simple majority outside Article 368.
tq: Identify the federal provisions first and reject the ordinary-law subject mixed into the list.
sec: ■ Provisions requiring state ratification - list, proportion, role of State Legislature  [other exams]

s:
Consider the following pairs:

List-I: Constitutional subject
A. Election of the President
B. GST Council
C. Representation of States in Parliament
D. Citizenship

List-II: Provision
1. Article 279A
2. Articles 54 and 55
3. Fourth Schedule
4. Article 11

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
o: A-2, B-1, C-3 and D-4
A-1, B-2, C-4 and D-3
A-2, B-3, C-1 and D-4
A-4, B-1, C-2 and D-3
x: Articles 54 and 55 concern the election of the President; Article 279A establishes the GST Council; the Fourth Schedule concerns representation of States in Parliament; Article 11 concerns citizenship.
tq: Start with the sure article-subject pairs and eliminate codes containing a misplaced provision.
sec: ■ Provisions requiring state ratification - list, proportion, role of State Legislature  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following was added to the category of provisions requiring State ratification by the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016?
o: The Inter-State Council under Article 263
The GST Council under Article 279A
The Finance Commission under Article 280
The Election Commission under Article 324
x: The 101st Amendment Act, 2016 added Article 279A relating to the GST Council to the federal provisions requiring State ratification.
tq: Use the amendment-year association and distinguish the GST Council from other constitutional bodies.
sec: ■ Provisions requiring state ratification - list, proportion, role of State Legislature  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the role of State Legislatures in constitutional amendment?
o: A State Legislature may refer an amendment Bill to the Supreme Court for approval.
A State Legislature cannot initiate a constitutional amendment; it can only ratify certain Bills passed by Parliament.
A State Legislature can initiate an amendment by passing a resolution under Article 368.
A State Legislature can introduce an amendment Bill in Parliament concerning a State subject.
x: States cannot initiate amendments under Article 368. Their role is limited to ratifying amendments concerning specified federal provisions; the creation or abolition of a Legislative Council follows Article 169 outside Article 368.
tq: Ask who has the initiating power and distinguish it from the State Legislature’s limited ratifying role.
sec: ■ Provisions requiring state ratification - list, proportion, role of State Legislature  [other exams]

s: The Supreme Court’s decision in Rajendra N. Shah (2021) is associated with which of the following?
o: Striking down Part IXB in its entirety for violating the federal structure without any further qualification
Invalidating the GST Council under Article 279A
Declaring the 24th Amendment unconstitutional for abridging Fundamental Rights
Striking down the provisions relating to State co-operative societies in Part IXB for want of ratification by the States
x: In Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the provisions of Part IXB relating to State co-operative societies were struck down for want of ratification by the required number of States.
tq: Match the judgment with the precise constitutional defect rather than the broad subject of federalism.
sec: ■ Provisions requiring state ratification - list, proportion, role of State Legislature  [other exams]

s:
Which of the following amendments to the Constitution can be made by Parliament by a simple majority and is not treated as an amendment under Article 368?
1. Formation of new States and alteration of their areas, boundaries or names
2. Creation or abolition of Legislative Councils in States
3. Change in the official language under Article 343
4. Amendment of the basic structure of the Constitution
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
x: Formation and alteration of States, Legislative Councils and official language provisions are among matters amendable by simple majority outside Article 368. The basic structure cannot be amended even by the special procedure.
tq: Spot the impermissible constitutional concept mixed with provisions amendable by ordinary law.
sec: ■ Amendments by simple majority outside Article 368 - which provisions  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following is NOT a provision that may be amended by a simple majority outside Article 368?
o: The distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States
Citizenship under Article 11
The number of puisne judges of the Supreme Court
The Fifth and Sixth Schedules
x: The distribution of legislative powers, including the Seventh Schedule, is a federal provision requiring the prescribed State ratification. Citizenship, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules and the number of puisne judges of the Supreme Court are amendable by simple majority.
tq: Find the federal provision that does not belong to the ordinary-law category.
sec: ■ Amendments by simple majority outside Article 368 - which provisions  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 327 — Elections and delimitation
Article 2 to Article 4 — Formation and alteration of States
Article 169 — Creation or abolition of Legislative Councils
Article 368 — Citizenship
x: Article 368 contains the general constitutional amendment procedure, whereas citizenship is among the matters that can be changed by simple majority under Article 11. Articles 2–4, 169 and 327 relate to the subjects stated.
tq: Use the wrong Article-subject pairing trap and verify the provision against the subject.
sec: ■ Amendments by simple majority outside Article 368 - which provisions  [other exams]

s:
Which of the following matters is included among those that can be changed by simple majority outside Article 368?
1. Quorum in Parliament
2. Salaries and emoluments of Members of Parliament
3. Privileges of Parliament and its members
4. The basic structure of the Constitution
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1, 2 and 3 only
1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only
x: Parliamentary quorum, salaries of MPs and parliamentary privileges are among provisions amendable by simple majority outside Article 368. The basic structure is beyond the amending power.
tq: Group the parliamentary procedural and administrative matters, then eliminate the basic-structure proposition.
sec: ■ Amendments by simple majority outside Article 368 - which provisions  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the method of amendment?
o: Representation of States in Parliament — simple majority outside Article 368
Citizenship — simple majority outside Article 368
Official language — special majority under Article 368 only
GST Council — simple majority as an ordinary law
x: Citizenship under Article 11 is amendable by simple majority outside Article 368. The GST Council and representation of States in Parliament are among provisions requiring State ratification.
tq: Compare the ordinary-law category with the federal-ratification category rather than relying on the subject’s importance.
sec: ■ Amendments by simple majority outside Article 368 - which provisions  [other exams]

s:
Arrange the following provisions in the order in which they are referred to in the Constitution, from the earliest Article number to the latest:
A. Creation or abolition of Legislative Councils
B. Citizenship
C. Elections and delimitation
D. Official language
o: B, A, C, D
A, B, D, C
B, C, A, D
A, C, B, D
x: The relevant provisions are Article 11 for citizenship, Article 169 for Legislative Councils, Article 327 for elections and delimitation, and Article 343 for official language.
tq: Order the items by Article number, not by the political importance of the subject.
sec: ■ Amendments by simple majority outside Article 368 - which provisions  [other exams]

s: The power of Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights was constitutionally affirmed in response to which judicial decision by the Constitution (24th Amendment) Act, 1971?
o: Minerva Mills case
Rajendra N. Shah case
Golaknath case
Kesavananda Bharati case
x: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 was enacted in response to Golaknath (1967), which had restricted Parliament’s power to amend Fundamental Rights.
tq: Link the constitutional amendment to the judgment it was designed to answer.
sec: ■ Limitations - basic structure, 24th Amendment, judicial review of amendments  [other exams]

s: What was the effect of the Constitution (24th Amendment) Act, 1971 on Articles 13 and 368?
o: It declared every constitutional amendment to be ordinary law under Article 13.
It empowered Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights and inserted Article 13(4), excluding an Article 368 amendment from the term ‘law’ in Article 13.
It prohibited Parliament from amending Fundamental Rights and removed Article 368.
It made all constitutional amendments subject to approval by a national referendum.
x: The 24th Amendment amended Articles 13 and 368, empowered Parliament to abridge or take away Fundamental Rights and inserted Article 13(4), under which an amendment made under Article 368 is not ‘law’ for Article 13.
tq: Test the paired effects of one amendment instead of confusing it with the later basic-structure judgments.
sec: ■ Limitations - basic structure, 24th Amendment, judicial review of amendments  [other exams]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Kesavananda Bharati judgment upheld the 24th Amendment.
2. The judgment held that Fundamental Rights and the Preamble cannot be amended under any circumstances.
3. The judgment held that the basic structure cannot be altered by constitutional amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Kesavananda Bharati upheld the 24th Amendment and held that the basic structure cannot be amended. It also held that Fundamental Rights and the Preamble are amendable, subject to the basic-structure limitation.
tq: Separate amendability of individual provisions from the unamendability of the basic structure.
sec: ■ Limitations - basic structure, 24th Amendment, judicial review of amendments  [other exams]

s:
Assertion (A): The amending power of Parliament is not unlimited.
Reason (R): The basic structure of the Constitution cannot be altered even by a constitutional amendment.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both statements are true, and the basic-structure limitation directly explains why Parliament’s constituent amending power is not unlimited.
tq: Check whether the Reason supplies the constitutional basis for the limitation stated in the Assertion.
sec: ■ Limitations - basic structure, 24th Amendment, judicial review of amendments  [other exams]

s:
The Constitution (42nd Amendment) Act, 1976 attempted to achieve which of the following in relation to the amending power?
1. To declare the amending power unlimited
2. To make constitutional amendments non-justiciable
3. To insert clauses (4) and (5) in Article 368
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: The 42nd Amendment inserted clauses (4) and (5) in Article 368, declared the amending power unlimited and attempted to bar judicial review of constitutional amendments.
tq: Treat the amendment number, clauses and legal effect as separate checks in a statement question.
sec: ■ Limitations - basic structure, 24th Amendment, judicial review of amendments  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of the Minerva Mills judgment, 1980?
o: It struck down the provisions making the amending power unlimited and excluding judicial review.
It declared the 24th Amendment wholly unconstitutional.
It upheld clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 as valid limitations on judicial review.
It held that the Preamble could not be amended.
x: Minerva Mills struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 inserted by the 42nd Amendment. It reaffirmed that limited amending power and judicial review are basic features.
tq: Match the judgment with the precise provision it invalidated, not with the earlier Golaknath dispute.
sec: ■ Limitations - basic structure, 24th Amendment, judicial review of amendments  [other exams]

s: Which of the following expressions is used in Article 368 to describe Parliament’s constituent power to amend the Constitution?
o: May, in exercise of its judicial power, interpret or repeal any provision
Shall, in exercise of its constituent power, amend every provision by referendum
May, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision
May, in exercise of its legislative power, repeal only those provisions approved by the States
x: Article 368 states that Parliament may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal of any provision, subject to the basic-structure limitation.
tq: Select the precise constitutional wording and reject substitutions of legislative or judicial power.
sec: ■ Limitations - basic structure, 24th Amendment, judicial review of amendments  [other exams]

s: The amendment procedure of the Indian Constitution has been borrowed from which country?
o: Ireland
Canada
South Africa
Australia
x: The amendment procedure of the Indian Constitution is generally identified as having been borrowed from South Africa.
tq: Use the source-country association specific to the amendment procedure rather than the source of another constitutional feature.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure → source country and criticism

s: Which one of the following best characterises the nature of the Indian constitutional amendment procedure?
o: It is entirely flexible because every provision can be changed by ordinary law.
It is rigid only in matters relating to Fundamental Rights.
It is a synthesis of rigidity and flexibility.
It is entirely rigid because every provision requires State ratification.
x: The Indian Constitution combines different methods of amendment and is therefore neither purely rigid nor purely flexible; it is a synthesis of both.
tq: Compare the constitutional system as a whole instead of applying one amendment method to every provision.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure → source country and criticism

s: Who described the constitutional amendment process as appearing ‘complicated’ but being ‘merely diverse’?
o: K. C. Wheare
R. Ambedkar
Granville Austin
Jawaharlal Nehru
x: Granville Austin described the process as appearing complicated but being merely diverse. He also called it one of the most ably conceived aspects of the Constitution.
tq: Distinguish the constitutional scholar associated with the exact evaluative description.

s: Which of the following is NOT a criticism commonly made of the constitutional amendment procedure in India?
o: States cannot initiate an amendment.
A joint sitting is available to resolve a deadlock between the two Houses on an amendment Bill.
There is no time limit for State ratification.
There is no special constitutional body or referendum for amendments.
x: The Constitution provides no joint sitting mechanism for resolving a deadlock between the Houses on an amendment Bill. The other three are recognised criticisms of the procedure.
tq: Look for the proposition that reverses an actual criticism by asserting that a safeguard exists.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure → source country and criticism

s:
Consider the following statements regarding criticisms of the constitutional amendment procedure:
1. Parliament alone can amend most constitutional provisions.
2. No outside constitutional convention or special body is required for amendment.
3. Ratification by the States is required for every constitutional amendment.
4. States cannot initiate an amendment under Article 368.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: Parliament alone amends most provisions, no special body or referendum is required, and States cannot initiate amendments. State ratification is required only for a limited group of federal provisions, not every amendment.
tq: Reject the absolute statement ‘every’ by distinguishing limited State ratification from general amendment practice.
sec: ■ Amendment procedure → source country and criticism

s: A constitutional amendment Bill affecting the representation of States in Parliament has been passed by Parliament. Which further constitutional requirement applies before it can be presented for Presidential assent?
o: Approval by a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament
Approval by all State Legislatures through special majority
Ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States by simple majority
A referendum held in the affected States only
x: Representation of States in Parliament is a federal provision. Its amendment requires ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States by simple majority; no joint sitting or referendum is prescribed.
tq: Apply the federal-provision test to the facts of the proposed amendment.

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the majority required under the Article 368 type of special majority?
o: Majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of the members present and voting in each House
Two-thirds of the total membership of each House
Two-thirds of the members present and voting in the Rajya Sabha only
Simple majority of the total membership of both Houses taken together
x: The Article 368 type requires both a majority of the total membership of each House and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in each House.
tq: Separate the total-membership requirement from the present-and-voting requirement.

s: The majority required for the impeachment of the President of India is
o: Two-thirds of the total membership of the House concerned
Two-thirds of the members present and voting in both Houses
Majority of the total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting in both Houses
Three-fourths of the total membership of Parliament
x: Under the Article 61 type of majority, impeachment of the President requires two-thirds of the total membership of the House concerned.

o: Article 61 only
Articles 249 and 312
Article 368 only

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Constitution of India combines rigidity and flexibility in its amendment procedure.
2. The basic-structure limitation permits judicial review of constitutional amendments.
3. Every provision of the Constitution can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: only certain provisions can be altered through the simple-majority route, while other provisions require special procedures and are subject to the basic-structure limitation.
tq: Reject the absolute claim that all constitutional provisions follow one amendment route.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding constitutional amendment proposals referred to in 2026:
1. The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, relating to women's reservation and delimitation, was negatived in the Lok Sabha.
2. The Delimitation Bill, 2026, was withdrawn.
3. The Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024, relating to simultaneous elections, was before a Joint Parliamentary Committee.
4. The Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2026, concerns removal of a Prime Minister, Chief Minister or Minister detained for 30 consecutive days for an offence punishable with five or more years of imprisonment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
x: All four statements are correct. The 131st Bill concerned women's reservation and delimitation, the Delimitation Bill was withdrawn, the 129th Bill was before a JPC, and the 130th Bill addressed continued detention of specified ministers for serious offences.
tq: Separate the subject and procedural status of each numbered Bill instead of treating all amendment proposals alike.

s: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, failed to secure the required two-thirds support among members present and voting primarily because
o: the Bill was required to be passed unanimously by both Houses
the number voting against was more than two-thirds of the total Lok Sabha membership
the Rajya Sabha rejected it by a two-thirds majority
the number voting in favour was 298 out of 528, which was less than two-thirds
x: Two-thirds of 528 is 352, whereas the Bill received only 298 votes in favour. It was negatived in the Lok Sabha; the stated vote was not a Rajya Sabha vote or a unanimity requirement.
tq: Apply the present-and-voting threshold numerically rather than comparing the result with total House strength.

s: Which one of the following best reflects the criticism and constitutional significance associated with the 2026 vote on the proposed amendment?
o: It established that a simple majority is always sufficient for constitutional amendment, although critics favour greater executive power.
It demonstrated that the basic structure can be altered whenever both Houses agree by a simple majority.
It showed that every constitutional amendment must be approved by a referendum, although critics oppose judicial review.
It showed that a special majority can protect constitutional change from being secured by a slim majority, although critics consider simple-majority routes too easy.
x: The vote was viewed as demonstrating the protective role of a special majority against a slim majority. At the same time, critics argue that routes using only a simple majority make constitutional change too easy.
tq: Match the two linked ideas—protection through special majority and criticism of easy simple-majority routes.
